Onboarding.title: Founder onboarding
Onboarding.subtitle: Tell us about your budget, capacity, and Lebanon sellability so we can guide one SKU.

Onboarding.storageLimitsPlaceholder: e.g. 2 free shelves; no boxes over 40cm; dry room; no fragile.

Onboarding.codComfortPlaceholder: e.g. Comfortable with COD; will track refusals.
Onboarding.codNoticeBody: COD means the buyer pays you in cash to the delivery person on arrival — not a payment to your China supplier. It is common in Lebanon and carries collection risk, refusal rates, and last-mile courier fees. Plan margins and cash flow accordingly.
Onboarding.sampleClearance: I am ready to handle sample clearance with a partner when needed (mainly for Import).
Onboarding.errorGeneric: Something went wrong. Check the form and try again.
Onboarding.couriersNote: Door delivery companies are chosen later in Store setup (placeholders until you confirm a real partner).
Onboarding.clearanceNote: Clearance partner: placeholder until you confirm a real partner. Matters most for Import — Local samples usually skip China customs.

info.budgetUsd: Total cash the OS assumes for your sample, first batch, and early ads. Fit and Margin guidance use this number. Minimum is $2,000.
info.monthlyFollowOn: What you can keep putting into ads and ops each month after launch. The OS uses it to size marketing spend estimates.
info.hoursPerWeek: Time you can spend on creatives and day-to-day ops. This sets your marketing creative capacity tier (how many assets per plan).
info.experience: A soft Fit ranking signal — not a grade. It nudges how aggressive or beginner-friendly Discovery products look for you.
info.maxLandedCost: Your per-unit ceiling for planning (product + shipping + clearance + courier). Discovery only shows products that can fit under this.
info.riskTolerance: A soft Fit signal for higher-risk or “Okay” products. It shapes ranking; it does not replace your judgment on what to accept.
info.sampleClearance: Means you can handle import clearance for a sample with a partner when needed. Most relevant for Import; Local Lebanon suppliers usually skip China customs. This is not last-mile door delivery to customers — you choose that later in Store setup.
info.storageLimits: Optional. Note anything that limits storage — available space, largest box you can keep, stairs or access, heat/humidity, or fragile/oversized items you can’t handle. We save this to your profile; smarter product suggestions from these notes come later with AI. It does not change product matching in v1.

Supplier.title: Choose a supplier — sample first
Supplier.intro: Two shortlists for this product: Import (China) and Local (Lebanon). Always get and approve a sample before you commit to a batch. This OS marks steps — you still contact suppliers and place real orders yourself. Local may be empty or partial when no reliable Lebanon listing is found.

shopifyCreated.title: Create your Shopify store
shopifyCreated.body:
In a browser:

• Go to shopify.com and start a store (trial is fine for setup).
• In Admin → Products → Add product: enter a title, USD price, and at least one photo (you can refine EN/AR copy in later steps).
• Pick a simple theme under Online Store → Themes — avoid heavy custom apps for v1.
• Copy your store URL into the Store URL field under Build in this OS. A *.myshopify.com address is enough for v1 — custom domain can wait.
• If menus look different, search Shopify Help for “create a store”, “add a product”, or “themes”.

Done when: You can open Admin, you have at least one product draft or listing, and you have saved your store URL here.

currencyUsd.title: Set store currency to USD
currencyUsd.body:
In Shopify Admin:

• Go to Settings → General → Store defaults.
• Choose Change store currency → USD → Save.
• Markets (customer presentment currencies) is separate — this step is your store’s default currency, not Markets.
• After real orders exist, store currency may be locked; you may need Shopify Support to change it.
• Still price products in USD for this OS — it is the stable reference for Lebanon founders.
• If labels differ, search Help for “change your store currency”.

Done when: Store defaults show USD and you price products in USD.

contentEnAr.title: Add EN + AR product content
contentEnAr.body:
In Shopify Admin → Products:

• Open your product (or create it).
• Starter EN/AR text lives under “Make the page stronger” below this checklist — Copy the drafts, then paste into Admin (this OS does not write to Shopify).
• Paste a clear English title + description from the EN draft (edit to match the real item).
• Add Arabic the same way — use the AR draft, or a translation app, then proofread.
• Add at least one real product photo.
• Themes differ for bilingual layout; some use a language app or separate metafields. Search Help for “multiple languages” if needed.

Done when: Shoppers can read the offer in English and Arabic on the product page.

productPublished.title: Publish the product
productPublished.body:
In Shopify Admin → Products → your product:

• Set Status to Active (not Draft).
• Under Publishing / Sales channels, include Online Store.
• Save.
• Open the product on the storefront to confirm it appears.

Done when: The product is Active and visible on the Online Store channel.

codPrimary.title: Enable cash on delivery (COD)
codPrimary.body:
In Shopify Admin:

• Go to Settings → Payments.
• Under Manual payment methods, add Cash on Delivery (COD). If labels differ, search Help for “manual payment methods” or “cash on delivery”.
• Make COD available at checkout for Lebanon buyers — this is your primary payment path in v1. No third-party COD app required.
• COD means the buyer pays you (cash to the delivery person) when the order arrives — not a payment to your China supplier, and not a marketing claim.
• New COD orders often stay Payment pending until you mark them paid after the delivery company confirms collection.

Done when: COD is enabled and appears as a checkout payment option.

optionalPayments.title: Optional local payments (or skip)
optionalPayments.body:
Optional — skip if COD-only. This checklist is honor-system (no Shopify API).

• In Settings → Payments, review any extra methods Shopify offers for your region (card, wallet, etc.).
• Only enable a method you can actually settle and support.
• If nothing usable appears, or you choose COD-only: do not enable a fake method — mark this item done when you decide to skip.
• Do not install random payment apps just to tick a box.

Done when: You enabled one real optional method you can settle, or you marked this done because you are skipping (COD-only).

courierSelected.title: Pick a last-mile delivery company
courierSelected.body:
Delivery company here means the last-mile company that delivers to the customer’s door in Lebanon — not China freight and not customs clearance.

• The Delivery company list under Build may be placeholders in v1 (including “I’ll confirm later”). Pick one for now, or your real door-delivery company when you have one.
• Save the choice in the Delivery company field under Build so Marketing/Finance know who delivers.
• Shipping rates in Shopify (go-live steps) are checkout prices — they are separate from which delivery company you hire.

Done when: A delivery company is selected and saved in the Delivery company field under Build.

shortPolicies.title: Add short policies
shortPolicies.body:
In Shopify Admin → Online Store → Pages (or Settings → Policies):

• Starter policy text lives under “Make the page stronger” below this checklist — Copy the policies draft, then paste into Admin (this OS does not write to Shopify).
• Add short Shipping, Returns, and Payment/COD pages — use the policies draft as a start.
• State clearly: pay the delivery person in cash on delivery; returns window; damaged/wrong item contact via WhatsApp.
• Link policies in the footer of your theme.
• Keep them short; buyers skim.

Done when: Shipping + returns (+ COD terms) are published and linked from the storefront.

whatsappConnected.title: Show WhatsApp to buyers
whatsappConnected.body:
Shopify has no native “connect WhatsApp” switch for this checklist.

• Put your WhatsApp number on the theme header, footer, or product page (button or plain text with wa.me link).
• Save the same number in the WhatsApp field under Build — Marketing creatives point buyers here.
• Test the link on your phone.

Done when: Buyers can tap/message WhatsApp from the storefront, and the number is saved in this OS.

sellToLebanon.title: Allow sales to Lebanon
sellToLebanon.body:
In Shopify Admin:

• Go to Settings → Markets.
• Include Lebanon as a country/market you sell and ship to (add or edit a market that covers Lebanon).
• Remove blocks that exclude Lebanon if any exist.
• If labels differ, search Help for “markets” or “sell to a country”.

Done when: Checkout accepts a Lebanon shipping address without a “we don’t ship here” error.

shippingRates.title: Set shipping rates
shippingRates.body:
Shipping rates = what the buyer pays (or sees as free) at checkout for delivery. They are not the same as choosing your delivery company.

• Go to Settings → Shipping and delivery.
• Add a rate (or free shipping) that covers Lebanon addresses for your product’s weight/size.
• Set product weight on the product if Shopify asks or rates look wrong.
• Keep rates simple for v1 — one nationwide band is fine.
• If menus differ, search Help for “shipping rates”.

Done when: Checkout shows a valid shipping option for a Lebanon address.

storePublic.title: Make the store public
storePublic.body:
In Shopify Admin:

• Go to Online Store → Preferences.
• Turn off password protection / “Restrict access to visitors with the password”.
• Shopify often requires selecting a pricing plan before password can be removed. Choosing a plan during trial typically does not charge until the trial ends. If the control is disabled, pick a plan first, then remove the password.
• Save.
• Verify in an incognito (private) window: open the storefront URL without logging into Admin — it must load without asking for a store password.
• If labels differ, search Help for “password protection” or “remove password”.

Done when: Incognito visitors can browse without a password gate.

testCheckout.title: Run a COD test checkout
testCheckout.body:
From an incognito window on the public storefront:

• Add the product to cart and checkout with a Lebanon address.
• Choose Cash on Delivery / COD — do not require a card.
• Place the test order (use a test name/phone you recognize).
• In Admin → Orders, confirm the order appears. COD orders often show as Payment pending until you mark them paid after real delivery company / delivery person collection.
• Cancel or fulfill the test order so it does not confuse real ops.

Done when: You see a COD test order in Admin → Orders.

Vocabulary.title: Vocabulary
Vocabulary.guidance: All phases stay open — read any term anytime. Sections follow the journey so you can focus where you are, without locking the rest.

sku.definition: The single product you import and sell. Lebanon Ecom OS is built around one active SKU at a time so decisions stay focused.

why.discovery: You pick and accept one SKU here — that choice becomes your working product for the rest of the journey.
why.sample_request: Supplier emails, MOQ, and sample checks all refer to this same SKU — don't switch mid-sample.
why.store_setup: Your Shopify product page, photos, and policies should describe this SKU clearly before you sell.
why.selling: Weekly numbers (ads, COD, courier) are judged against this SKU's margins — stay with it until you intentionally change.

fit.meaning: How well a product matches you
fit.definition: A score of how well a catalog product matches your budget, capacity, experience, and Lebanon sellability. The OS uses it to rank what you see first.

why.discovery: Fit steers the shortlist — stronger matches rise so you waste less time on products you can't run.

strongFit.definition: A product that clears your hard filters and scores well on budget, margins, and capacity. Treat it as a serious candidate, not a maybe.

why.discovery: Strong-fit cards are your best first looks — shortlist them before spending hours on weaker options.

okayFit.definition: A product that passes the basics but has trade-offs (tighter margin, harder ops, or weaker demand). Worth a look, not automatic accept.

why.discovery: Okay-fit items fill the list when strong fits are few — compare carefully before you accept one.

demandSignal.definition: Clues that buyers in Lebanon (or similar markets) already look for this kind of product — search interest, marketplace presence, or proven niches.

why.discovery: The OS surfaces demand signals so you don't pick a SKU that only looks cheap — it should be sellable too.

differentiation.definition: What makes your offer different enough to win — kit, brand angle, bundle, or positioning — so you're not a pure price race on commodity goods.

why.discovery: Weak differentiation means paid ads get expensive fast. Prefer SKUs where you can say something clear and ownable.

tier1Marketplace.definition: A large, well-known marketplace (think Amazon-class). Products already winning there often have clearer demand — but also more copycats.

why.discovery: Tier-1 presence is a demand clue, not a copy-paste plan. The OS may ask you to customize or drop if it's too crowded.

landedCost.meaning: All-in cost per unit in Lebanon
landedCost.definition: What one unit really costs after product, freight, clearance, and last-mile into your hands. Margins in the OS are judged against landed cost, not factory price alone.

why.discovery: Early landed-cost estimates decide if a SKU can clear the 70% / 35% margin gates before you accept it.
why.sample_approved: After the sample, enter real quotes so landed cost stops being a guess before you mark a batch ordered.
why.batch_ordered: Your batch cash outlay is landed cost × units — keep ETA and clearance in view so the number stays honest.

marginBeforeAds.definition: Gross margin after landed cost and selling costs, before you spend on ads. The OS expects about 70%+ here so ads have room to work.

why.discovery: If before-ads margin is thin at accept time, the SKU is likely a no — don't hope ads will fix a bad unit economy.
why.sample_approved: Update costs after the sample; confirm before-ads margin still holds before you commit batch cash.
why.selling: Topic A weeks compare real results to this target — if it collapses, pause spend and fix price or costs.

marginAfterAds.definition: What's left after ad spend on top of landed and selling costs. The OS looks for roughly 35%+ after ads as a healthy floor while selling.

why.discovery: After-ads margin is the reality check — a pretty before-ads number that dies once you advertise won't pass.
why.selling: Weekly health uses after-ads margin to coach spend: cut, hold, or invest next based on what you actually earned.

showMore.definition: A control that reveals additional curated products when your first batch isn't enough. It widens options without dumping the whole catalog at once.

why.discovery: Use Show more when the first cards don't fit — the OS still ranks by fit instead of random scrolling.

curatedCatalog.definition: The OS product list already filtered for Lebanon-friendly, importable SKUs. You still judge fit and margins — curation only removes obvious non-starters.

why.discovery: You're choosing inside a curated set, not the whole internet — faster decisions with fewer regulatory landmines.

activeSku.meaning: The product you're focusing on now
activeSku.definition: The product currently driving supplier and marketing deep-links. Shop Topic A (Finance) stays store-wide across every selling SKU — it is not private books for the active SKU alone.

why.discovery: Accepting a product sets the active SKU — supplier and marketing tools follow that choice.
why.selling: Open a SKU for product tools; log weeks in Shop Topic A for the whole store’s combined health.

approvalGate.definition: A required founder decision the OS won't skip — accept product, sample decision, batch marks, store ready, and similar. Automation stops; you approve.

why.discovery: Accepting a product is an approval gate — once you say yes, the OS advances and treats that SKU as active.
why.sample_request: The sample decision gate (approve / reject / stuck path) unlocks batch and parallel setup — don't mark a batch without it.

sample.meaning: A paid test unit before the batch
sample.definition: A small paid order you request to check quality before any first batch. The OS tracks the request; you still contact the supplier yourself.

why.sample_request: Mark the sample here, email the supplier, then quality-check — this is the sample-first rule in action.

sampleFirst.meaning: Never batch before a good sample
sampleFirst.definition: A hard rule: approve a sample before you mark a first batch ordered. It protects cash from shipping a full MOQ of a bad product.

why.sample_request: The OS blocks batch flow until sample is approved — treat that lock as a feature, not friction.

supplier.meaning: The factory or seller you buy from
supplier.definition: The Import (often China) or Local (Lebanon) partner who quotes, ships samples, and fulfills your batch. You negotiate and email them; the OS stores facts and drafts.

why.sample_request: Pick Import or Local primary and backup suppliers here, then mark which one you actually sampled.

primarySupplier.meaning: First-choice card for your first sample
primarySupplier.definition: On the shortlist, the primary ranking marks who you usually sample first (Mode A). After approve, your working/path supplier is what matters for batch — that may be this primary. Other same-source cards can become warmed spares later without replacing working until you mark can’t-fulfill.

why.sample_request: Sample the primary first; only rotate if quality or negotiation fails.
why.sample_approved: After approve, batch follows the working path — not every “primary” label on the shortlist.

backupSupplier.meaning: A ranking label on shortlist cards — not an automatic path switch
backupSupplier.definition: Primary vs backup is ranking on the shortlist, not “you already switched path.” After path lock, any same-source card that is not the working supplier can be a spare (see Warmed spare) — primary/backup rank does not block spare sample CTAs. A backup card is not a warmed spare until its sample is approved.

why.sample_request: If the primary fails the sample gate, try another shortlist card (often the backup rank) before abandoning the SKU.
why.sample_approved: After path lock, use same-source non-working cards for spare insurance — rank alone does not warm them.
why.selling: While selling, spare insurance still uses approved samples on non-working cards — not the backup label by itself.

workingSupplier.meaning: The supplier path you’re buying on for this SKU
workingSupplier.definition: After the first sample is approved, this is your locked path for batch / next-batch. Approving a spare sample does NOT change it.

why.sample_approved: Know who your path is — spare approvals are insurance, not a silent switch.
why.batch_ordered: First batch and cost quotes follow the working supplier, not every warmed spare.
why.selling: Shop hub shows Working supplier per product — restock and path stay on this until can’t-fulfill.

warmedSpare.meaning: A backup with an approved sample ready if path fails
warmedSpare.definition: Request spare sample on a same-source card that is NOT the working supplier, then approve it. Insurance only — does not switch path. Aim for at least 2 when you can.

why.sample_approved: Warm a spare while your path is fine — saves weeks if they can’t fulfill later.
why.batch_ordered: You can still warm spares while the first batch ships — path stays put.
why.selling: Hub shows spares ready per product; use them only after can’t-fulfill, not as a casual switch.

importVsLocal.meaning: Where you source this SKU’s suppliers
importVsLocal.definition: Import (e.g. China) vs Local (Lebanon) supplier pools — tabs Import | Local | Both. Spare/switch stay same-source (Import↔Import or Local↔Local). Local cost fields differ; last-mile courier stays in Topic A.

why.sample_request: Pick Import or Local (or Both) before sampling so shortlist and quotes match the pool you can actually buy from.
why.sample_approved: Spare insurance and can’t-fulfill switches stay same-source — don’t mix Import path with a Local spare.

moq.definition: The smallest batch the supplier will sell. MOQ × landed cost is the cash you lock when you order — size it to budget and storage.

why.discovery: High MOQ can kill an otherwise good SKU if your $2k+ budget can't cover sample + first batch safely.
why.sample_request: Confirm MOQ in writing with the supplier while sampling — don't discover a surprise minimum at batch time.
why.batch_ordered: Your first batch quantity should respect MOQ without over-ordering past what you can store and sell.

unitPrice.definition: What the supplier charges per unit before freight and clearance. It's only one slice of landed cost — never judge margin on unit price alone.

why.sample_request: Capture unit price from quotes and negotiation so later cost worksheets stay accurate.

negotiation.definition: Working the supplier on unit price, MOQ, shipping terms, or extras (labels, packing). Small wins here compound across the whole batch.

why.sample_request: Negotiate while the sample is in play — leverage is weaker after you've already committed to a large order.

qualityChecklist.meaning: What to inspect on the sample
qualityChecklist.definition: A practical list for finishing, materials, sizing, packaging, and defects. Use it before you approve — photos help if you reopen the decision later.

why.sample_request: Approve only after the checklist passes; a vague "looks fine" is how bad batches get ordered.

clearance.definition: Getting the goods legally through Lebanese customs. Partner, fees, and paperwork belong in your landed-cost math and arrival plan.

why.sample_request: Ask early how samples and batches clear — surprise clearance fees wreck margins.
why.batch_ordered: While inventory is in transit, line up clearance so arrival doesn't stall in port.
why.batch_received: After arrival, confirm clearance is done before you treat stock as ready to sell.

cashLock.meaning: Money tied up until you sell
cashLock.definition: Budget trapped in sample, deposit, freight, or inventory before revenue returns. The OS watches locks so you don't over-commit past your runway.

why.sample_request: A sample is a small intentional lock — better than locking a full MOQ on an untested product.

stuckPath.definition: A guided branch when suppliers fail, cash is tight, or the sample loop isn't converging — including higher-stakes path options the OS surfaces for approval.

why.sample_request: If you're looping suppliers without progress, use the stuck path instead of silently burning weeks.

sampleApproved.definition: The human gate after a good sample. It unlocks batch ordering and parallel tracks (store + intro marketing) without forcing store readiness first.

why.sample_approved: You're here because quality passed — next is real costs, batch mark, and parallel setup, not another sample delay.

introMarketing.definition: The first marketing kit after sample approval — teach basics and warm creative direction before heavy paid spend.

why.sample_approved: Start intro marketing in parallel with costs and store work so you're not learning ads the week stock arrives.

parallelNextSteps.meaning: Workstreams that run side by side
parallelNextSteps.definition: After sample approval you can advance batch, store, and marketing together. Store readiness is a side status — it never blocks marking a batch ordered.

why.sample_approved: Don't wait for a perfect store to order stock; run the tracks in parallel and keep batch moving.

costQuotes.definition: Founder-entered quotes for freight, clearance, and courier that replace discovery estimates. They refresh expected margin and batch cash needs.

why.sample_approved: Enter quotes before you mark batch ordered — fake freight numbers create false confidence.

batchVsSample.definition: A sample proves quality; a batch is sellable inventory at MOQ scale. Never treat a sample carton as your launch stock plan.

why.sample_approved: Approval means quality is good enough to buy a batch — it is not the same as having inventory to sell.

shopify.definition: The storefront where Lebanon customers browse and check out. The OS tracks setup progress; you build and connect payments and delivery yourself.

why.store_setup: Store readiness lives here as a checklist — finish Shopify basics while the batch is elsewhere in the journey.

storeReadiness.definition: A side-status percentage of Shopify checklist progress. Important for launch quality — but it never gates marking a batch ordered.

why.store_setup: Push readiness up in parallel; don't stall the import spine waiting for 100%.

cod.definition: Customers pay when the courier delivers. Common in Lebanon, but it creates outstanding cash and return risk you must track weekly.

why.store_setup: Wire COD into checkout and delivery so launch isn't blocked by payment confusion.
why.selling: COD outstanding is working capital — Topic A weeks watch it so "sales" don't hide unpaid deliveries.

localPayments.definition: Local methods like Whish and OMT that many buyers prefer alongside or instead of cards. Offer what your customers already use.

why.store_setup: Add local rails during store setup so conversion isn't stuck on card-only checkout.

deliveryCompany.definition: The Lebanon courier that picks up, delivers, and often collects COD. Fees and failed-delivery rates hit after-ads margin.

why.store_setup: Choose and connect a courier before launch so orders don't pile up unshipped.

policyPages.definition: Store pages that set expectations on returns, delivery, and data. They reduce disputes and make paid traffic feel safer.

why.store_setup: Tick policy pages on the readiness checklist before you push hard paid traffic.

whatsappCommerce.definition: Using WhatsApp for questions, order confirmations, and sometimes closing sales — expected buyer behavior in Lebanon.

why.store_setup: Put a clear WhatsApp path on the store so hesitant COD buyers can ask before they order.

sideStatus.meaning: Progress that doesn't block the spine
sideStatus.definition: Tracks like store readiness that matter operationally but do not control the primary journey advance (sample → batch → sell).

why.store_setup: Store work is a side status — finish it seriously, but never use it as an excuse to delay a justified batch order.

batch.definition: The first real stock order after sample approval — sized around MOQ and budget. You place it externally; the OS records that you ordered.

why.batch_ordered: Marking batch ordered tells the OS inventory is in motion — ETA, pre-launch marketing, and arrival gates follow.

firstBatch.definition: The initial MOQ-scale order that funds launch. Keep it lean enough to learn, large enough to not stock-out in week one.

why.batch_ordered: While waiting on arrival, plan launch creatives against first-batch quantity — not infinite stock.

preLaunchMarketing.definition: Creatives and audience warming after batch is ordered but before arrival. Stay inside the paid cap — you're not in full selling mode yet.

why.batch_ordered: Use the transit window to warm demand so launch week isn't cold traffic on day one.

paidCap.definition: A ceiling on pre-launch / early paid spend so you don't burn budget before inventory can fulfill orders.

why.batch_ordered: Respect the paid cap while stock is in transit — hype without inventory creates refunds and COD pain.

inventoryInTransit.meaning: Stock that has shipped but not arrived
inventoryInTransit.definition: Units you've paid for (or committed to) that are between factory and your shelves. Track ETA and clearance; they're cash lock until received.

why.batch_ordered: This is your main status while waiting — don't mark arrived until goods are actually in hand and clearable.

eta.definition: When you expect the batch to land. The OS uses it to pace pre-launch work and to flag when arrival is overdue.

why.batch_ordered: Keep ETA updated so marketing and store launch timing stay realistic.

inventory.definition: Physical stock available (or soon available) to fulfill orders. Inventory ties cash, storage, and how hard you can advertise.

why.batch_ordered: In-transit inventory is almost sellable — plan launch volume against units on the water, not wishful extras.
why.batch_received: Arrived inventory unlocks ready-to-sell — count units before you scale ads.
why.selling: Weekly health should reflect stock left; selling hard into empty shelves wastes ad spend.

batchArrived.definition: You mark that the first batch is in Lebanon and usable. It unlocks finance preview and the path toward selling.

why.batch_received: Mark arrived only when goods are truly here — that gate turns transit hopes into sellable reality.

readyToSell.definition: Inventory is received and you're operationally able to take orders (store, delivery, payments far enough along). Launch marketing can go live.

why.batch_received: Confirm ready-to-sell before blasting ads — orders without fulfillment destroy trust and COD rates.

launchKit.definition: Creatives and guidance for opening paid/organic push once stock can fulfill. Stronger than intro marketing — meant for real demand.

why.batch_received: Pull the launch kit when arrived and ready — this is the creative set for first selling weeks.

preSalesEstimate.definition: A rough forecast of early sales based on batch size, price, and planned spend. Use it to set week-one targets, not as a promise.

why.batch_received: Compare the estimate to first Topic A weeks later — learning beats clinging to the forecast.

topicA.definition: The shop-combined weekly finance loop once you're selling — log spend, COD, courier, and per-SKU sales so the OS can coach margins and invest-next. Not a private P&L for one product.

why.selling: Do Shop Topic A every week; skipped weeks hide bleed until cash is gone.

topicB.definition: The product-focused view of your active SKU economics and facts — companion to weekly Topic A, not a replacement.

why.selling: Open Topic B when unit economics look off — price, landed cost, or offer may need a change.

weeklyHealth.meaning: How the business looked this week
weeklyHealth.definition: A compact read of margins, cash movement, and risk signals from your Topic A inputs. It's the coaching pulse, not a vanity dashboard.

why.selling: Read weekly health before raising ad spend — it tells you whether last week earned the next dollar.

codOutstanding.definition: Money still with customers or couriers from COD orders not yet remitted. It inflates "sales" until it hits your account — or returns.

why.selling: Track COD outstanding weekly so you don't spend ads against cash you don't actually have.

adSpend.definition: What you spent on paid traffic in the period. After-ads margin only works if this number is honest and complete.

why.selling: Log ad spend in Topic A every week — missing spend makes margins look healthier than they are.

courierFees.definition: Per-order or weekly fees from your delivery partner, including failed-delivery costs. They sit in selling costs and shrink margin.

why.selling: Include courier fees in weekly logs; ignoring them quietly kills the 35% after-ads floor.

investNext.meaning: Where to put the next dollar
investNext.definition: OS coaching on whether to raise ads, fix offer/creative, cut spend, or free cash — based on the week you just logged.

why.selling: Follow invest-next as a decision aid after Topic A; don't raise spend on autopilot.

nextBatch.definition: A side-flow on Selling — mark next batch ordered with the same working supplier (bookkeeping). Not the first batch; does not rewind the journey to batch_ordered.

why.selling: Use next batch when runway or invest-next says restock — keep it distinct from your first batch journey.

cantFulfillSwitch.meaning: How you change working supplier while selling
cantFulfillSwitch.definition: If the working supplier can’t fulfill a restock, mark can’t-fulfill on that SKU’s Supplier panel, then pick a warmed spare (same source). Stay on Selling — path changes only then.

why.selling: This is the only switch moment — warming a spare is not a path change until you mark can’t-fulfill.

addSku.meaning: Start another product in the same shop
addSku.definition: Opens discovery for a new live product in one Shopify workspace. Gates by experience (beginner needs healthy Topic A streak; some warn; experienced after first accept). Each SKU has its own supplier/marketing journey.

why.discovery: You’re adding another product to the same shop — not opening a second store.
why.selling: Add SKU from the hub when experience and Topic A health allow — each product keeps its own supplier path.

archiveSku.meaning: Hide a live product without wiping history
archiveSku.definition: Archive removes it from live hub focus; restore brings it back. Wipe forever is a separate permanent step. Shop Topic A history stays.

why.selling: Archive from the hub when a product should pause out of live focus — restore if you need it again.

conversion.definition: The rate at which store traffic turns into paid (or COD) orders. Weak conversion burns ad spend even when the product is fine.

why.selling: If conversion drops, refresh creative and page before blaming the SKU — creative fatigue often shows up here first.

creativeFatigue.definition: When the same creatives wear out and performance falls. Lebanon audiences are small — fatigue shows up faster than in huge markets.

why.selling: Weekly refresh fights fatigue; don't wait until after-ads margin collapses to rotate creatives.

weeklyRefresh.definition: A habit of updating ads/offers each week so messaging stays fresh. Pairs with Topic A so you change creative from evidence, not boredom.

why.selling: Schedule a weekly refresh alongside Topic A — small creative changes beat rare big redesigns.

Shop.introEmpty: Start by discovering and accepting your first product. Once you have more than one, this hub becomes your shop overview.
Shop.shopPausedBanner: Shop is paused from the top bar — every SKU shows as paused until you resume there.
Shop.sparesNoneYet: Spares ready: none yet — warm at least 2 when you can
Shop.sparesSwitchNote: Warming a spare does not switch your working supplier. If they can’t fulfill, open that product’s Supplier → Supplier can’t fulfill → pick a warmed spare.
Shop.addSkuIntro: Open discovery for a new product. Gates depend on your experience and shop Topic A health.
Shop.addSkuDiscoveryBanner: Adding another product — your live SKUs and shop journey stay as they are.
Shop.archivedHint: Archive is reversible — Restore brings the product back with its history. Wipe forever is permanent and only available after archive.
Shop.archivedSkuBanner: This product is archived. Restore to continue its journey (reversible), or Wipe forever (permanent — cannot be undone).
Shop.skuSubline: This SKU’s spine — sample, batch, and selling.
Shop.archiveConfirm: Archive this SKU? You can restore it later with full history. Shop Topic A history stays. Wipe forever is a separate, permanent step after archive.
Shop.wipeConfirm: Wipe forever? This permanently deletes the SKU and cannot be undone. Wipe is only available after archive — Restore will no longer be possible.
Shop.unitsLeftUnknown: Units received aren’t known yet for this product.
Shop.unitsLeftUnknownHint: Mark the batch arrived in Supplier once inventory is in.

gate.beginner_blocked: As a beginner, add a second SKU only after ≥15 healthy Topic A weeks and the last 5 all healthy.
gate.early_add: Warning: you’re adding early before the Topic A bar — continue carefully.
